To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
metal transport dynamics from the bulk solution to the biointerfaces and the kinetics of internalisation control the toxicological responses of microorganisms to metals.

(i) BLM underestimates the time-dependent metal toxicity to bacteria, (ii) metal internalisation kinetics is the main factor controlling the metal partitioning at the cell surface, (iii) the cell surface electrostatic properties and the cell density are the key factors governing the metal partitioning dynamics, (iv) metal internalisation is a key factor controlling the metal-induced cell growth and death kinetics.
metal toxicity is controlled by metal partitioning at the biointeface and the metal internalisation kinetics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a generalised theory of metal toxicity to micro-organisms that accounts for coupled toxicodynamic and interfacial partitioning processes.

the development of a novel mechanistic framework that integrates metal transport dynamics, cell surface properties and metal-induced cell growth dynamics for a comprehensive understanding of metal toxicity at biointerphases.
the formulation of an advanced mechanistic theory for metal partitioning and toxicodynamics at the biointeface, which is beyond the BLM framework.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

metal toxicity to microalgae is a complex process that cannot be fully understood without a rigorous mechanistic understanding of metal transport to the biosurface, metal internalisation, and cell growth inhibition.

the classical BLM is not suitable to predict the time-dependent metal toxicity to microalgae and bacteria, and that a more rigorous theoretical framework is needed to account for metal transport dynamics at the biointerior and the metal-induced cell growth and cell size variations.
BLM is an appropriate tool to predict the toxicity of a given metal to a microorganism under steady-state exposure conditions, but it is not adequate to predict metal toxicity over time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the classical BLM framework is insufficient to account for time-dependent metal toxicity to microalgae and bacteria.
the Biotic Ligand model framework is not adequate to describe metal toxicity to micro-organisms over time, unless metal transport kinetics and cell growth dynamics are accounted for.
metal partitioning at cell interfaces is a key process to consider when evaluating metal toxicity to microalgae and other aquatic microorganisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that

metal toxicity is a function of time-dependent metal partitioning and metal internalisation kinetics at the biosurface, and that these processes need to be accounted for in a mechanistic manner in the context of the Biotic Ligand Models.
the metal internalisation dynamics at the biosurface is a critical factor in the evaluation of metal toxicity to microalgae and microorganisms in general.
the BLM framework is insufficient in predicting the toxicity of metal ions to microorganisms over time.
